title: Bridging ML and algorithms: comparison of hyperbolic embeddings
one_liner: The algorithm from the computer science algorithms community is 100 times faster than machine-learning methods while producing equally good or better embeddings of hierarchical networks.
lead: Hyperbolic space is a mathematical structure where distances grow exponentially as you move away from the center, fitting hierarchical structures like trees naturally. Two research communities study how to convert networks and hierarchies into embeddings (numerical vectors) in this space: computer scientists and machine learners. They developed different algorithms independently and never directly compared them. This paper compares performance and quality head-to-head, finding that an algorithm from the algorithms community vastly outperforms the popular machine-learning embeddings that were widely accepted as the best approaches because it uses direct mathematical construction instead of slow iterative optimization.

problem.h2: Two communities, separate algorithms, no comparison
paras: Hyperbolic embeddings map networks and hierarchies into vectors (lists of numbers) using hyperbolic space, where the amount of room available expands exponentially as you move away from center, naturally fitting tree-like hierarchies. Computer scientists and machine learners both study this problem, but they work independently and publish in separate venues, so they never directly tested which approach is faster or produces better embeddings.

A naive approach would be to try each method and hope for the best, but practitioners did not know how much time or quality they were sacrificing. The popular machine-learning approaches (Poincaré embeddings from NIPS 2017 and Lorentz embeddings from ICML 2018) were well-cited, so most practitioners assumed they were close to optimal. Without a direct benchmark, no one knew a simpler algorithm from the algorithms community was available.

callout.html: The paper directly measures and compares the speed and quality of hyperbolic embedding algorithms across both research communities on real networks.

panels.title: 1. Hyperbolic space: natural for trees
panels.viz_args: A network with hierarchy: root at center, levels expand outward like rings.
panels.caption: Hierarchical networks have exponential branching—hyperbolic space fits this naturally.

panels.title: 2. Two separate communities, same problem
panels.caption: ML methods are famous; algorithms method is unknown. No direct comparison exists.

panels.title: 3. Compute embeddings: who is fastest?
panels.caption: Speed comparison: Blsius method is vastly faster than ML approaches.

panels.title: 4. Measure quality: how good are embeddings?
panels.viz_args: Rank preservation: does the learned space keep similar nodes close? Hierarchy coverage: does it respect tree structure?
panels.caption: Quality metrics test whether the embedding captures the original network structure.

panels.title: 5. Result: Blasius wins on both fronts
panels.caption: Faster and just as accurate—the algorithms method dominates.

steps.text: Collect real-world hierarchies and networks, plus simulated networks with known structure.
Apply Blsius (algorithms), Poincaré (ML), and Lorentz (ML) to each network and measure wall-clock time.
Test how well each method preserves hierarchy and proximity: do close nodes stay close in the embedding?
Compute the speedup: wall-clock time for Blsius divided by time for each ML method.
Show that Blsius is 100x faster because it avoids iterative optimization, while achieving equal or better quality.

paras: This paper does not propose a new algorithm—it brings an existing algorithm from the computer science algorithms community into direct comparison with the dominant machine-learning methods. By benchmarking all three side-by-side on the same networks with the same quality metrics, it reveals that the prior belief (that ML methods were best) was based on incomplete information.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: computational cost per embedding
hidden.name: Computation time to embed a network
paras: Computational cost is how long the algorithm takes (in seconds or minutes) to convert a network into embeddings. Machine-learning methods like Poincaré and Lorentz use gradient descent—a slow iterative process where the algorithm starts with random guesses and gradually improves them by nudging each number in a direction that reduces error. The Blsius algorithm, by contrast, uses direct construction based on mathematical principles: it builds the embedding by solving mathematical problems directly, without iteration. This makes it much faster because each iteration of gradient descent touches every node and every edge, multiplying the cost by the number of iterations needed to converge; Blsius avoids that multiplication entirely.

The paper measures cost by running each method on the same hardware and timing wall-clock seconds. It also records memory usage. The dramatic speed difference—100x—comes from the gap between iterative refinement (slow) and direct mathematical solution (fast).

heat.caption: Hotter means slower or more costly. Blsius is cold on time and memory, warm on quality.

reads.html: It takes 100 seconds to embed a network with Poincaré, but 1 second with Blsius. The embedding quality is almost identical.
Algorithm by Blsius et al computes embeddings in linear time via direct geometric construction; Poincaré and Lorentz use random gradient descent, which is quadratic or worse.

mechanism.h2: Why Blsius is so much faster
paras: Poincaré and Lorentz embeddings use gradient descent, an iterative optimization loop. The algorithm starts with random numbers (coordinates in hyperbolic space) and repeatedly adjusts them—compute how far off we are from the target, compute which direction to nudge each number, nudge it, repeat thousands of times until the error stops shrinking. Each iteration touches every node and every edge, so the total time grows as iterations multiplied by network size. With thousands of iterations needed to converge, this is slow.

Blsius uses a different strategy: it constructs the embedding in a single pass using mathematical rules. It starts at the center of hyperbolic space and places nodes by computing the angular distance that represents proximity in the original network, placing each node at that angle, then scaling its distance from center to match its hierarchy level. No iteration is needed; the construction is direct. This runs in linear time—proportional to the number of nodes, not quadratic or worse.

stages.s: ML approach: initialize random coordinates, loop 1000 times: compute error, nudge each number downhill
Algorithms approach: compute angles and radii directly via mathematical rules, place nodes in one pass

math.words: In hyperbolic space, the distance between two points is not Euclidean. Instead, it grows exponentially with the radius. The closer a point is to the center, the more space is packed around it. This naturally represents hierarchies because roots are central and branches spiral outward, with each level having more space.
math.equation: d_hyp(u, v) = arccosh(cosh(r_u) * cosh(r_v) - sinh(r_u) * sinh(r_v) * cos(theta_diff))
symbols: distance between points u and v in hyperbolic space
distance from center (radius) for each point

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Point A at radius 2.0, angle 0 degrees: r_A = 2.0, theta_A = 0
Point B at radius 3.0, angle 90 degrees: r_B = 3.0, theta_B = 90
Angle difference theta_diff = 90 degrees (convert to radians: pi/2 ≈ 1.57)
Interpretation: the distance is 4.63 in hyperbolic metric—much larger than straight-line distance would predict, because hyperbolic space expands.

math.note: Blsius computes these radii and angles once per node using geometric rules; ML methods adjust them thousands of times via gradient descent.

charts.title: Wall-clock time (seconds)
charts.note: Lower time is better because faster embedding means practitioners can process larger networks interactively. Blsius is 100x faster because it avoids iterative loops.

charts.title: Embedding quality (hierarchy preservation, 0-100)
charts.note: Quality is nearly identical—Blsius actually edges out the ML methods in some tests.

items.html: If the network is a dense random graph (not tree-like), hyperbolic embeddings of any kind will be poor because hyperbolic space is built for hierarchies. The paper tests on hierarchies and tree-like networks, so this is a limitation.

The hyperbolic functions (cosh, sinh, arccosh) can overflow for large radii if computed carelessly. Blsius and the ML methods must use numeric libraries that handle large hyperbolic radii safely, or embeddings will become invalid.

Poincaré and Lorentz embeddings can get stuck in local minima (suboptimal solutions) depending on random initialization. Poor initialization leads to poor embeddings. Blsius avoids this entirely by using mathematical rules, not optimization.
When benchmarking, ensure all three methods use the same network data, the same hardware, the same quality metrics, and enough iterations for ML methods to converge. The paper does this carefully.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: A demo should take a hierarchical network (for example, a category taxonomy or a tree of topics), embed it using all three methods, and plot wall-clock time and quality scores. The key is to vary network size—small, medium, large—so the 100x speedup becomes visible as the network grows. Record memory usage too. A good demo would also visualize the resulting embeddings (plot them as a 2D projection) to show that all three methods produce similar-looking embeddings, just at different speeds.
demo.metric_eq: speedup = time_poincare / time_blasius,  quality_difference = quality_blasius - quality_poincare
demo.closing: The demo must make it impossible to miss that Blsius wins decisively on speed with no sacrifice in quality.
